name: A01: Broken Access Control
evidence: Multiple authenticated routes with ID parameters (e.g., GET /api/Users/:id, GET /api/Cards/:id, DELETE /api/Cards/:id) use inconsistent or missing authorization: some enforce security.appendUserId() or security.isAuthorized(), but others (e.g., GET /api/Recycles/:id, GET /api/Deliverys/:id, GET /rest/products/:id/reviews) have auth: null and no middleware enforcing ownership or role checks — enabling potential BOLA. Also, auto-CRUD routes like /api/Users/:id expose full model attributes (excluding only 'password'/'totpSecret') without per-field or per-role property-level enforcement.

name: A02: Cryptographic Failures
evidence: JWT usage confirmed via 'express-jwt' and 'jsonwebtoken' (v0.4.0 — outdated), TOTP in 2FA flows (twoFactorAuth.* handlers), password handling in /api/Users registration flow, and presence of encryptionkeys directory served publicly (/encryptionkeys/:file via serveKeyFiles). No evidence of secure key storage, key rotation, or modern hashing (e.g., bcrypt/scrypt); legacy jsonwebtoken v0.4.0 is highly vulnerable to algorithm confusion and weak defaults.

name: A03: Injection
evidence: File upload handlers process YAML (js-yaml v3.14.0 — known for arbitrary code execution via unsafe load()), XML (libxml2-wasm v0.7.1 — susceptible to XXE if parser misconfigured), and ZIP archives (handleZipFileUpload). No evidence of safe parsing (e.g., js-yaml.loadSafe, XXE-disabled libxml2 config). Also, raw SQL queries absent but ORM (Sequelize) used — however, auto-CRUD routes lack input sanitization guarantees, and client-side innerHTML/bypassSecurityTrustHtml (28 occurrences) enables DOM-based XSS, a client-side injection vector.

name: A04: Insecure Design
evidence: Architecture shows functional patterns (e.g., rate limiting on reset-password, 2FA setup, access control hooks) but lacks design artifacts (threat models, abuse cases, business logic specs). While flawed implementations exist (e.g., undocumented /api/Quantitys with denyAll but exposed via auto-CRUD), insecure design requires analysis of *intent* vs *spec*, which architecture alone cannot confirm.

name: A05: Security Misconfiguration
evidence: Public exposure of sensitive directories: /ftp (with icons/view=details), /.well-known (with static serving + index), /encryptionkeys (with file listing + serveKeyFiles), /support/logs (with serveLogFiles + index). Also, CORS is configured (via 'cors' v2.8.5) but no configuration details provided — risk of overly permissive origin; 'helmet' v4.6.0 is present but version is outdated (v7+ recommended), and feature-policy (deprecated) is used instead of Permissions-Policy.

name: A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
evidence: Outdated dependencies confirmed: jsonwebtoken v0.4.0 (should be ≥9.x), js-yaml v3.14.0 (v4+ fixes RCE), express-rate-limit v7.5.1 (v7.10+ fixes bypasses), helmet v4.6.0 (v7+ required for modern headers), libxml2-wasm v0.7.1 (XXE risks), and multer v1.4.5-lts.1 (v1.4.5 has known DoS via malicious zip). 117 total deps, 24+ security-relevant — high likelihood of known CVEs.

name: A07: Identification and Authentication Failures
evidence: Login (/rest/user/login), password reset (/rest/user/reset-password), 2FA setup/verify/disable, security question flow, and session-less auth patterns (e.g., JWT tokens implied by express-jwt). Critical gaps: no evidence of brute-force protection on login (only on reset-password & 2FA endpoints), no logout endpoint, no session expiration, no credential stuffing mitigation, and password repeat validation only as challenge — not enforced server-side universally.

name: A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures
evidence: YAML deserialization (js-yaml) and XML parsing (libxml2-wasm) are high-risk deserialization surfaces. Web3/NFT endpoints (/rest/web3/*) accept untrusted inputs (e.g., wallet addresses, keys, contract exploits) and invoke walletNFTVerify, contractExploitListener — implying dynamic code/data evaluation. Also, auto-CRUD exposes model schemas directly, risking mass assignment if excludeAttributes isn’t strictly enforced at runtime.

name: A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
evidence: Metrics endpoint (/metrics) exists and is served twice (lines 668 & 720), and metrics.observeFileUploadMetricsMiddleware is used — confirming telemetry infrastructure. However, no evidence of audit logging (e.g., failed logins, privilege changes, data exports), no SIEM integration, no anomaly detection, and logs are publicly listable (/support/logs with serveIndexMiddleware) — indicating insufficient monitoring depth and confidentiality.

name: A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
evidence: No explicit outbound HTTP client usage (e.g., axios, node-fetch) visible in route definitions or middleware names. However, /rest/web3/* endpoints (walletNFTVerify, contractExploitListener, nftMintListener) and /b2b/v2/orders suggest external integrations; absence of evidence ≠ absence of SSRF-prone calls. Architecture does not reveal URL construction logic or fetch patterns.

name: API1: Broken Object Level Authorization
evidence: Direct object references with IDs (e.g., /api/Users/:id, /api/Cards/:id, /api/Addresss/:id) are widely exposed. Many lack ownership validation: e.g., GET /api/Addresss/:id uses security.appendUserId() but no check that :id belongs to the user; similarly, /rest/memories POST uses appendUserId() but GET /rest/memories has auth:null — enabling horizontal privilege escalation. Auto-CRUD routes compound this with generic, non-ownership-aware handlers.

name: API2: Broken Authentication
evidence: Authentication is fragmented: some endpoints use security.isAuthorized(), others security.appendUserId(), some use custom middleware (e.g., twoFactorAuth.*), and many (e.g., /rest/user/whoami, /rest/user/authentication-details) have auth:null but rely on implicit session/JWT — yet no global auth guard. Password reset lacks binding to user context (no token binding to session/IP), and 2FA setup/verify occurs without re-authentication. JWT library version (0.4.0) is critically outdated.

name: API3: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
evidence: Auto-CRUD routes (e.g., /api/Users/:id) exclude 'password' and 'totpSecret' — good — but expose all other fields (e.g., email, lastLoginIp, isAdmin) without field-level RBAC. Endpoints like GET /api/Users return full user lists (line 358) with auth:security.isAuthorized() but no role scoping — allowing low-privilege users to enumerate admins. No evidence of property-level filtering per role (e.g., 'isAdmin' hidden from regular users).

name: API4: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
evidence: Rate limiting applied only selectively: /rest/2fa/*, /rest/user/reset-password, and /rest/user/login (implied by login() middleware) — but absent on high-cost endpoints like /api/Users (list all users), /rest/products/search, /rest/order-history/orders (accounting-only but no rate limit), and file uploads (/file-upload has size checks but no per-IP or burst limits). Also, /metrics is publicly accessible and could be abused for scraping.

name: API5: Broken Function Level Authorization
evidence: Function-level access controls are inconsistent: /api/Products/:id DELETE uses security.denyAll(), but /api/Products POST uses security.isAuthorized() — implying any authorized user can create products, yet none can delete. Similarly, /api/Quantitys/:id DELETE uses security.denyAll(), but /api/Quantitys/:id PUT uses security.isAccounting() + IpFilter — exposing function-level bypass risk if IP filter is trivially spoofed. Admin functions (e.g., /rest/order-history/:id/delivery-status) lack secondary approval or logging.

name: API6: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
evidence: Sensitive flows lack safeguards: /rest/user/data-export allows export without CAPTCHA or step-up auth despite containing PII; /rest/2fa/setup enables TOTP enrollment without re-authentication; /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress accepts arbitrary contract addresses; /ftp and /encryptionkeys expose infrastructure artifacts; and /the/devs/are/so/funny/... paths indicate deliberate obfuscation over proper access control.

name: API7: Server Side Request Forgery
evidence: Same rationale as A10 — no direct evidence of fetch/axios usage or dynamic URL construction in route definitions. Web3 and B2B endpoints suggest external calls, but implementation details (e.g., whether walletNFTVerify resolves user-supplied URLs) are absent from architecture.

name: API8: Security Misconfiguration
evidence: API-specific misconfigs: Swagger docs cover only 1 of 148 routes (/b2b/v2/orders), leaving 109 hand-written + 28 auto-CRUD endpoints undocumented — increasing attack surface via unknown behaviors. Public API docs (/api-docs) expose internal structure. Also, /rest/admin/application-configuration and /rest/admin/application-version leak stack details. No evidence of API versioning, deprecation policies, or request validation (e.g., JSON schema).

name: API9: Improper Inventory Management
evidence: Swagger documents only 1 path; 109 hand-written and 28 auto-CRUD routes are undocumented — violating API inventory best practices. Hidden endpoints like /the/devs/are/so/funny/..., /this/page/is/hidden/..., and /we/may/also/instruct/... confirm intentional obscurity over proper inventory. Auto-CRUD routes expose internal model names (e.g., 'Quantitys', 'Addresss') and pluralizations inconsistent with REST norms — indicating poor governance.

name: API10: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
evidence: Architecture shows no client-side API consumption patterns (e.g., frontend calling external 3rd-party APIs). All listed endpoints are backend-internal or server-rendered. LLM tooling uses internal functions (searchProducts, getOrderById), not external APIs — so 'consumption' here is intra-app, not cross-domain.

name: LLM01: Prompt Injection
evidence: Genuine tool-calling confirmed (searchProducts, getProductReviews, getOrderById, generateCoupon) with Zod validation and real side-effects. However, no evidence of prompt sanitization, output parsing guards, or sandboxing — making tools susceptible to adversarial prompting that manipulates tool arguments or bypasses validation (e.g., injecting MongoDB operators into searchProducts input).

name: LLM02: Sensitive Information Disclosure
evidence: LLM tools execute database queries (Sequelize + MongoDB) and return raw results (e.g., getOrderById returns full order objects). If tool outputs are reflected unfiltered in LLM responses (e.g., via streamText), PII (addresses, emails, payment methods) or system details (e.g., from application-configuration) could leak. No evidence of output redaction, field filtering, or response hardening.

name: LLM03: Supply Chain
evidence: LLM dependencies include @ai-sdk/openai-compatible v2.0.35 and ai v6.0.116 — both actively maintained but subject to transitive vulnerabilities. More critically, tools depend on internal modules (e.g., payment.getPaymentMethods, address.getAddress) whose integrity relies on the broader app supply chain (e.g., sequelize v6.37.3, outdated jsonwebtoken) — creating cascading trust boundaries.

name: LLM05: Improper Output Handling
evidence: Client-side Angular components use 28 bypassSecurityTrustHtml/innerHTML assignments — many tied to dynamic content (e.g., search-result, product-details, feedback-details). If LLM-generated or API-sourced content (e.g., product reviews, feedback, chat responses) flows into these sinks without sanitization, XSS occurs. No evidence of DOMPurify, sanitize-html (used elsewhere but not in LLM output path), or contextual escaping.

name: LLM06: Excessive Agency
evidence: Tools have high-privilege capabilities: generateCoupon creates redeemable coupons, getOrderById accesses arbitrary orders (no ownership check shown), and searchProducts may expose full catalog. No evidence of agency constraints (e.g., max coupon discount, order scope limiting, search result pagination caps) — enabling LLM-driven abuse like mass coupon generation or order enumeration.

name: LLM10: Unbounded Consumption
evidence: No rate limiting or quota enforcement visible on LLM endpoints (/rest/chat, /rest/web3/*). Tools like searchProducts and getOrderById can trigger expensive DB queries; generateCoupon has no issuance limits. Combined with public /rest/chat access and no concurrency controls, this enables resource exhaustion (CPU, DB connections, memory).
